notes: Ruling slot 23 = Alaouite monarchy under Hassan II (state of exception since 1965). UNFP moved from MD's USFP slot 3 (no popularity) to 18 (popularity); slot 3 holds the ICFTU-affiliated UMT. MD placements kept: UGTM 6, MP 13, Istiqlal 14, CGEM 15 (moved from MD 7 as an employers' body), PDI 20, FAR 22. Oufkir's security apparatus in 0, MPDC in 1, Guedira's PSD in 2, PLS in 4, Fqih Basri's armed Tanzim in 7, Shabiba Islamiyya (founded 1969) in 12. No Moroccan Shia: slots 8/9 are small Alid-devotional and Najaf-student circles.

0.name: Clan Oufkir
0.text:
The Oufkir Clan is the security apparatus built by General Mohamed Oufkir, Minister of the Interior and the most feared man in Morocco after the king. With his deputy Ahmed Dlimi of the national security service, he crushed the 1965 Casablanca riots and was convicted in absentia by a French court for the abduction of Mehdi Ben Barka.

The clan stands for repression of the left, control of elections through the provincial administration and close cooperation with American, French and Israeli intelligence. Loyal to the throne in words, it accumulates power in its own right. Its leverage lies in the police, the governors, the secret detention centres and files on every politician.

1.name: Mouvement populaire démocratique et constitutionnel
1.text:
The Popular Democratic and Constitutional Movement was founded in 1967 by Dr Abdelkrim al-Khatib, a former leader of the Liberation Army and president of the parliament dissolved in 1965, after he broke with the Popular Movement. Khatib opposed the state of exception, and his small party survives as a royalist but constitutionalist voice.

The MPDC defends the monarchy, Islam and the Arab-Berber heritage while demanding a return to parliamentary life, honest administration and social justice. Firmly anti-communist and Western-leaning, it counts on Khatib's personal ties to the palace and to veterans of the resistance. Its base is small: notables, former fighters and pious professionals.

2.name: Parti socialiste démocrate
2.text:
The Democratic Socialist Party was founded in 1964 by Ahmed Reda Guedira, the king's closest political adviser and architect of the 1962 constitution, after the collapse of his royalist Front for the Defence of Constitutional Institutions. Despite its name, it is a liberal party of the palace, small and dormant under the state of exception.

It favours a constitutional monarchy with a strong king, a liberal economy open to foreign investment, a modern administration and alliance with France and the United States. Its members are francophone lawyers, senior officials and businessmen. Its leverage is Guedira's influence with Hassan II and the drafting of the new constitution the palace is preparing.

3.name: Union marocaine du travail
3.text:
The Moroccan Labour Union was founded in March 1955 and is led by Mahjoub Ben Seddik. It is the largest trade union of the country, a member of the ICFTU, and helped create the UNFP in 1959, but since the mid-1960s it has distanced itself from party politics to protect its organization from repression.

The UMT pursues collective bargaining, higher wages, social security and the Moroccanization of jobs in mines, railways, ports and the phosphate industry. It favours social reform and cautious bargaining with the palace over confrontation. Its leverage is the strike weapon in Casablanca and the mining centres, and its financial and organizational strength.

4.name: Parti de la libération et du socialisme
4.native_full: Parti de la libération et du socialisme
4.text:
The Party of Liberation and Socialism was formed in 1968 by Ali Yata as the legal successor of the Moroccan Communist Party, banned since 1960. It was dissolved by the authorities in 1969 and its leaders prosecuted, so it works in semi-clandestinity among intellectuals, teachers and workers.

The PLS follows Moscow, calls for national democratic revolution, agrarian reform, nationalization of key industries and the restoration of democratic liberties. Unusually, it supports Moroccan claims to the Sahara and seeks a patriotic alliance with the national movement. Its leverage lies in the Casablanca intelligentsia, parts of the student movement and Soviet bloc support.

5.name: Union nationale des étudiants du Maroc
5.native_full: Union nationale des étudiants du Maroc
5.text:
The National Union of Moroccan Students was founded in 1956 and is the most radical mass organization in the country. Its members marched against the throne in March 1965, and since then its congresses have become forums for the new revolutionary left that is growing impatient with the parties of the national movement.

The union demands democratic freedoms, the release of political prisoners, the truth about Ben Barka, educational reform and radical land reform, and supports the Palestinian and Vietnamese struggles. Many militants now look beyond the UNFP and PLS to Marxism-Leninism. Its leverage lies in strikes in the high schools and the university of Rabat.

6.name: Union générale des travailleurs du Maroc
6.native_full: Union générale des travailleurs du Maroc
6.text:
The General Union of Moroccan Workers was founded in 1960 by the Istiqlal Party as a rival to the UMT after the left split from the party. It organizes workers in commerce, administration, artisan trades and Fez's traditional industries, and is led by Istiqlal cadres loyal to Allal al-Fassi.

The UGTM combines Arab and Islamic nationalism with labour demands, calls for Arabization, the recovery of Moroccan territories still held by Spain and the elimination of foreign economic domination. It is anti-communist but sharply critical of Western influence. Its leverage is the Istiqlal machine and the conservative urban working class.

7.name: Al-Tanzim al-Sirri
7.text:
The Secret Organization is the armed network of Mohamed Basri, known as al-Fqih, a former resistance leader and founder of the UNFP. Condemned for conspiracy and now in exile, he organizes cells of former resistance fighters inside Morocco and trains volunteers in friendly Arab capitals, independent of the party's legal leadership.

The organization seeks to overthrow the monarchy by insurrection and to establish a revolutionary republic aligned with the Arab progressive camp against Western imperialism, with land reform and nationalization of foreign capital. Its leverage is a clandestine underground in the Middle Atlas and the cities, and support from Algiers, Damascus and the new regime in Tripoli.

8.name: Muhibbu Ahl al-Bayt
8.text:
The Lovers of the Prophet's House are a small circle of Idrisid shurafa, Sufi scholars and students in Fez and Moulay Idriss Zerhoun who emphasize Morocco's ancient attachment to the descendants of Ali, beginning with Idris I, the Alid refugee who founded the first Moroccan dynasty. They read Shia authors with curiosity while remaining Sunni.

They advocate a reformed, spiritually inward Islam, dialogue with Shia scholarship, social justice drawn from Ali's example and respect for the sharifian heritage. They avoid politics and stay loyal to the throne. Their only leverage is the prestige of sharifian lineage and access to the religious milieu of Fez.

9.name: Talabat al-Najaf
9.text:
The Students of Najaf are a handful of Moroccans who encountered Shia teaching while studying in Iraq and Lebanon and returned with books and loyalty to the Najaf seminaries. They meet discreetly in Tangier, Fez and Casablanca, wary of a state whose religious legitimacy rests on the Sunni Maliki rite.

They believe that just rule belongs to learned clerics, condemn the monarchy's Western alliances and see the Sunni establishment as a servant of power. Their numbers are tiny and the security services would treat them as foreign agents. Their only leverage is the radical appeal of their ideas to students searching for revolutionary Islam.

10.name: Rabitat Ulama' al-Maghrib
10.text:
The League of Moroccan Ulama was founded in 1960 under the leadership of Shaykh Abdallah Guennoun of Tangier to unite the country's religious scholars. It brings together judges, preachers and teachers of the Qarawiyyin and the traditional schools under the protection of the king as Commander of the Faithful.

The league defends the Maliki rite, Arabic education, public morality and the religious legitimacy of the Alaouite throne, while warning against communism and Western permissiveness. It supports the monarchy but criticizes moral laxity and asks for a greater role of religion in law and schooling. Its leverage is religious authority and Friday sermons across the kingdom.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir al-Islami
11.text:
Hizb ut-Tahrir, the Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqi al-Din al-Nabhani, reaches Morocco through students returning from the Middle East and from European universities. Its sympathizers form only a few isolated study circles, without public presence.

The party seeks the restoration of a single caliphate over all Muslims, rejects nationalism, monarchy and republic alike as un-Islamic and condemns both Western and Soviet influence. It hopes to convert officers and intellectuals who could hand it power. Its leverage in Morocco is negligible, but its literature offers a revolutionary vision to young Muslims disillusioned with both palace and opposition.

12.name: Al-Shabiba al-Islamiyya
12.text:
Islamic Youth was founded in 1969 in Casablanca by Abdelkrim Moti, a school inspector, and fellow teachers inspired by Hassan al-Banna and Sayyid Qutb. Still small and unregistered, it recruits high-school and university students in Casablanca and Rabat to counter the influence of the Marxist left.

The movement calls for an Islamic society, the application of the sharia, moral discipline and Arabic education, and is fiercely hostile to communism and to Western cultural influence. Its stance toward the monarchy is ambiguous. Its leverage lies in schools, mosques and youth camps, and in the authorities' interest in an Islamist counterweight to the student left.

13.name: Al-Haraka al-Sha'biyya
13.text:
The Popular Movement was founded in 1957 by Mahjoubi Aherdane and veterans of the Liberation Army to represent the Berber countryside against the urban Istiqlal. Legalized in 1959, it became a pillar of the palace's governing coalitions and its notables continue to serve the king under the state of exception.

The movement defends the monarchy, rural interests, Berber culture and local notables, and opposes the centralizing Arabism of the national movement. It is pragmatic and loyal rather than ideological. Its leverage is a network of rural notables, tribal leaders and former resistance fighters in the Rif and the Atlas, indispensable to the palace in any election.

14.name: Hizb al-Istiqlal
14.text:
The Istiqlal Party led the struggle for independence after its manifesto of January 1944 and is led by Allal al-Fassi. After the left split away in 1959 and the party left government in 1963, it has stood in opposition, demanding the end of the state of exception imposed in 1965.

Istiqlal stands for constitutional monarchy, Islamic and Arab identity, Arabization, economic Moroccanization and a Greater Morocco including the Sahara and Mauritania. It is non-aligned and wary of both blocs. Its base is the bourgeoisie of Fez and Rabat, merchants, religious scholars and the UGTM, and it remains the best organized party in the country.

15.name: Confédération générale économique marocaine
15.text:
The General Economic Confederation of Morocco is the employers' federation inherited from the protectorate, still dominated by French-owned firms but increasingly joined by Moroccan industrialists, bankers and Fassi trading families of Casablanca. It speaks for big business under the state of exception.

The confederation favours private capital, foreign investment, low taxes, stable labour relations and close economic ties with France and the European Economic Community. It fears the Moroccanization demanded by Istiqlal and the UNFP only where it threatens its members' control. Its leverage is capital, export earnings and the personal links between big business, the palace and senior officials.

16.name: Les Épiciers soussis
16.text:
The Soussi Grocers are the Berber traders from the Sous valley and the Anti-Atlas whose family shops and wholesale houses dominate retail trade in Casablanca and the northern cities. Bound by kinship and village solidarity, they have built a commercial network from the corner shop to import firms.

They want freedom of trade, low taxes, cheap credit, protection of private property and a state that leaves commerce alone. Politically cautious, they back whoever guarantees order and keep their distance from the parties. Their leverage lies in their control of everyday distribution and in the savings they channel back into the Sous and into new businesses.

17.name: Institut scientifique chérifien
17.text:
The Sharifian Scientific Institute in Rabat, founded in 1920 under the protectorate, is the centre of natural science research in Morocco. Its botanists, zoologists and geologists study the Atlas cedar forests, the wetlands and the wildlife of the kingdom, alongside the foresters who manage the national parks of Toubkal and Tazekka.

Its scientists warn against deforestation, overgrazing, soil erosion and the drying of springs, and call for protected areas, reforestation and rational management of water. They are apolitical and cooperate with French and international scientific bodies. Their leverage is technical authority within the ministries of agriculture and water, rather than public mobilization.

18.name: Al-Ittihad al-Watani li-l-Quwwat al-Sha'biyya
18.text:
The National Union of Popular Forces was founded in 1959 by Mehdi Ben Barka, Abdallah Ibrahim and Abderrahim Bouabid when the left broke away from Istiqlal. Its leaders were prosecuted for alleged plots in 1963, Ben Barka was abducted in Paris in 1965, and the party now survives in opposition, divided between Bouabid's Rabat wing and Ibrahim's union-backed Casablanca wing.

The UNFP calls for an elected constituent assembly, agrarian reform, planning, nationalization of key sectors and non-alignment with the Third World. It rejects royal absolutism without openly demanding a republic. Its base is teachers, civil servants, workers and students, and its leverage lies in urban mobilization and international prestige.

19.name: Souffles
19.text:
Souffles is the circle around the cultural review founded in 1966 by the poet Abdellatif Laâbi, which has moved from avant-garde literature to revolutionary politics. Laâbi, the engineer Abraham Serfaty and young militants grow increasingly critical of the PLS leadership and its accommodation with the national movement.

The circle advocates a Marxist-Leninist revolution independent of Moscow, inspired by Vietnam, Palestine and China, and denounces both the monarchy and the reformist opposition. It champions popular culture, the Arabic and Berber languages and the self-determination of the peoples of the Sahara. Its leverage lies among students and young intellectuals in Rabat and Casablanca.

20.name: Hizb al-Shura wa-l-Istiqlal
20.text:
The Democratic Party of Independence was founded in 1946 by Mohamed Hassan Ouazzani, a pioneer of the nationalist movement and longtime rival of Allal al-Fassi. It shared in the independence struggle but was overshadowed by Istiqlal, and in 1970 it is a small party relying on Ouazzani's reputation.

The PDI appeals to popular resentment against the Istiqlal bourgeoisie and the new elite, calling for democracy, consultation, honest government and attention to the poor and the provinces. It supports the monarchy as a guarantor against single-party domination. Its leverage lies in Ouazzani's personal following in Fez and the north and in the palace's interest in dividing the nationalist camp.

21.name: Al-Maghrib al-Kabir
21.text:
Greater Morocco is the milieu of irredentist ultras, former Liberation Army fighters and nationalist officers who believe the kingdom's historic borders reach Mauritania, the Spanish Sahara, Tindouf and beyond. They are furious that Rabat signed the Ifrane treaty with Algeria in January 1969 and recognized Mauritania in September 1969.

They demand the liberation of the Sahara by arms, rejection of the colonial borders and a militarized nation united under a warrior king. Hostile to Spain, Algeria and the left, they despise compromise diplomacy. Their leverage lies among resistance veterans, Saharan exiles in the south and officers who see territorial expansion as the army's mission.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Malakiyya
22.text:
The Royal Moroccan Armed Forces were created in 1956 from Moroccan units of the French and Spanish armies and former resistance fighters, and Hassan II commanded them as crown prince. Their officers, many trained in France, fought Algeria in the 1963 Sand War, and senior generals such as Mohamed Medbouh, head of the royal military household, are among the king's closest aides.

The army is pledged to the throne and to the defence of the kingdom's territorial claims, and its officers prize order, discipline and American and French equipment. Yet many resent corruption at court and political dependence. Its leverage is decisive: it is the ultimate guarantor, and potential threat, to the monarchy.

23.name: Al-Usra al-Malakiyya al-Alawiyya
23.text:
The Alaouite Dynasty has ruled Morocco since the seventeenth century and claims descent from the Prophet. King Hassan II, enthroned in 1961, suspended parliament and declared a state of exception in June 1965, and since then he governs directly through appointed ministers, the Interior Ministry and the makhzen, with Ahmed Laraki as prime minister.

The monarchy presents itself as the arbiter above parties, the Commander of the Faithful and the guardian of national unity and territorial claims. It is anchored in the Western camp, relying on France and the United States, while keeping working relations with the Arab world. Its power rests on the army, the notables and religious legitimacy.
